Formal mathematical derivation proving that each step requires scanning at most k * T(n) cells, resulting in total single-tape simulation time O(T(n)^2).

topics.title: DECIDABLE VS UNDECIDABLE PROBLEMS
topics.plain: A problem is decidable if there exists an algorithm that always halts with a correct Yes/No answer. It is undecidable if no algorithm can ever be written that is guaranteed to solve it for all inputs.
topics.def: A decision problem P is a question with a boolean answer (Yes/No), represented as a formal language L_P = {w | answer for instance w is Yes}. P is Decidable if L_P is a recursive language (there exists a TM that halts on every w in Sigma* and outputs Yes or No). P is Undecidable if no such halting TM can exist. Cantor's Diagonalization method demonstrates that because the set of languages (2^(Sigma*)) is uncountably infinite while the set of Turing machines is countably infinite, undecidable languages mathematically must exist.
topics.exam: Always cite Cantor's Diagonal argument: Countable set of TMs vs Uncountable set of languages implies there are infinitely many problems that cannot be solved by any computer.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Confusing an intractable problem (e.g. exponential time O(2^n)) with an undecidable problem. Intractable problems CAN be solved algorithmically given enough time; undecidable problems can NEVER be solved by ANY algorithm regardless of time.
topics.example: Testing whether a given DFA accepts the empty string is decidable (BFS search). Testing whether a given Turing machine accepts the empty string is undecidable.
topics.q: Why does Cantor's Diagonalization principle prove the theoretical existence of undecidable computational problems?
topics.a: Because the set of all Turing machines is countably infinite, whereas the set of all possible languages is uncountably infinite (|P(Sigma*)| > |TM|).

topics.title: THE HALTING PROBLEM
topics.sub: Turing's Proof of Undecidability by Contradiction
topics.plain: Can we write a master program that looks at any code and its input, and tells us if it will ever halt or run forever? Alan Turing proved this is mathematically impossible.
topics.def: The Halting Problem language is HALT_TM = {<M, w> | M is a TM and M halts on input w}. Proof of Undecidability: Assume a decider H exists such that H(<M, w>) accepts if M halts on w, and rejects if M loops. Construct machine D: on input <M>, run H(<M, <M>>). If H accepts, D enters an infinite loop; if H rejects, D halts and accepts. Running D on its own description <D>: D halts on <D> iff D loops on <D>, an impossible logical paradox. Hence H cannot exist.
topics.exam: In ASTU exams, memorize the 3-step proof: (1) Assume decider H exists; (2) Construct adversarial machine D that inverts H(M, M); (3) Feed <D> into D to derive the self-referential contradiction D halts <=> D loops.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Believing the Halting Problem is unsolved. It is not an unsolved engineering challenge; it is proven to be mathematically IMPOSSIBLE to solve.
topics.example: An IDE cannot provide a 100% reliable warning that an arbitrary 'while' loop in Python or C will terminate.
topics.q: What logical contradiction occurs when the adversarial machine D (which inverts the Halting decider H) is executed on its own encoding <D>?
topics.a: D halts if and only if D loops forever (D halts <=> D does not halt), which is an impossible contradiction.

topics.title: MAPPING REDUCTIONS (MANY-ONE REDUCTIONS)
topics.plain: Reduction converts an instance of a known impossible problem into an instance of a new problem. If we could solve the new problem, we could solve the impossible problem—proving the new problem must also be impossible!
topics.def: Language A is mapping reducible to language B (written A <=_m B) if there exists a computable function f: Sigma* -> Sigma* such that for all w in Sigma*, w in A <=> f(w) in B. Key theorems: (1) If A <=_m B and B is decidable, then A is decidable; (2) If A <=_m B and A is undecidable, then B is undecidable; (3) If A <=_m B and A is not RE, then B is not RE.
topics.exam: Directionality matters! To prove target problem B is undecidable, you MUST reduce FROM a known undecidable problem A (like HALT_TM) TO problem B (A <=_m B). Reducing B to A proves nothing about B's undecidability!
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Reversing the reduction direction. Reducing target problem B to A only proves B is no harder than A; it does NOT prove B is undecidable.
topics.example: To prove that testing if a TM accepts the empty string (A_empty) is undecidable: reduce from A_TM. Given <M, w>, construct M' that ignores its input and runs M on w. Then w in A_TM <=> M' in A_empty.
topics.q: To prove that a new problem B is undecidable using a known undecidable problem A, what reduction must be constructed?
topics.a: You must reduce problem A to problem B (A <=_m B), showing that a decider for B would yield a decider for A.

topics.title: RICE'S THEOREM
topics.sub: Undecidability of Semantic Properties of RE Languages
topics.plain: Rice's theorem is a devastating result: ANY question about what a computer program actually computes (its language or output behavior) is undecidable, unless the question is trivial.
topics.def: Rice's Theorem: Let P be a property of Recursively Enumerable languages (i.e. P is a set of RE languages). P is non-trivial if there is at least one RE language with property P and at least one RE language without property P. Then the language L_P = {<M> | L(M) has property P} is UNDECIDABLE. In other words, any non-trivial semantic property of the language recognized by a Turing Machine is undecidable.
topics.exam: Semantic property (about L(M)) vs Syntactic property (about M): Rice's theorem applies ONLY to semantic properties (e.g. 'Does L(M) contain empty string?', 'Is L(M) regular?'). It does NOT apply to syntactic properties of the machine itself (e.g. 'Does M have > 5 states?' is DECIDABLE by inspection).
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Applying Rice's theorem to syntactic questions like 'Does M have 10 states?' or 'Does M ever transition to state q3?'. That is a property of the machine code, not the language L(M)!
topics.example: Testing whether a program's output language is empty (L(M) = phi), finite, regular, or context-free are ALL undecidable by direct application of Rice's Theorem.
topics.q: Why does Rice's Theorem NOT apply to the question: 'Does a given Turing Machine M have more than 7 states?'
topics.a: Because having > 7 states is a syntactic property of the machine's code/structure, whereas Rice's Theorem applies strictly to semantic properties of the language L(M).

topics.title: POST CORRESPONDENCE PROBLEM (PCP)
topics.sub: Domino Matching & The Undecidability of String Tiling
topics.plain: PCP is a game of dominoes with strings on the top and bottom. Can you arrange a sequence of dominoes (repeats allowed) so that the string on top matches the string on the bottom?
topics.def: An instance of the Post Correspondence Problem (PCP) consists of two lists of strings of equal length over alphabet Sigma: A = (x1, x2, ..., xk) and B = (y1, y2, ..., yk). A match is a sequence of indices i1, i2, ..., im (with m >= 1 and 1 <= ij <= k) such that x_i1 x_i2 ... x_im = y_i1 y_i2 ... y_im. Theorem: PCP is UNDECIDABLE when |Sigma| >= 2. However, PCP over a unary alphabet (|Sigma| = 1) is DECIDABLE.
topics.exam: Modified PCP (MPCP) requires the match to begin with the first pair (i1 = 1). MPCP is reduced from the Turing machine acceptance problem (by encoding computation histories), and MPCP is then reduced to standard PCP.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Assuming PCP is undecidable for unary alphabets. If |Sigma| = 1, strings represent lengths; PCP reduces to finding integer solutions to a linear Diophantine equation, which is DECIDABLE.
topics.example: Dominoes: (b, ca), (a, ab), (ca, a), (abc, c). Match: pairs (2, 1, 3, 2, 4) produce identical strings on top and bottom.
topics.q: Under what condition is the Post Correspondence Problem (PCP) algorithmically DECIDABLE?
topics.a: When the alphabet Sigma is unary (|Sigma| = 1), where the problem reduces to linear Diophantine integer equations.

topics.title: UNDECIDABLE DECISION PROBLEMS IN CFGs
topics.plain: While membership in a CFG is decidable (CYK algorithm), checking whether a grammar is ambiguous or whether two grammars produce the same language are completely undecidable.
topics.def: Decidability status of Context-Free Grammar problems: (1) Decidable: Membership (w in L(G)? via CYK in O(n^3)), Emptiness (L(G) = phi?), Finiteness; (2) Undecidable (proven via reduction from PCP): (a) Ambiguity: Is CFG G ambiguous? (b) Universality: Is L(G) = Sigma*? (c) Equivalence: Is L(G1) = L(G2)? (d) Intersection Emptiness: Is L(G1) cap L(G2) = phi? (e) Regularity: Is L(G) a regular language?
topics.exam: High-yield contrast table: For Regular Languages, Equivalence (L1 = L2) is DECIDABLE. For Context-Free Languages, Equivalence (L1 = L2) is UNDECIDABLE.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Believing ambiguity in CFGs can be checked by an algorithm. The question 'Is an arbitrary CFG G ambiguous?' is provably UNDECIDABLE.
topics.example: In compiler construction, we cannot write an automated tool that determines whether an arbitrary grammar provided by a developer is ambiguous.
topics.q: Name three fundamental decision problems for Context-Free Grammars that are provably UNDECIDABLE.
topics.a: 1. Testing if a CFG is ambiguous; 2. Testing if two CFGs are equivalent (L(G1) = L(G2)); 3. Testing universality (L(G) = Sigma*).

topics.title: THE CHOMSKY HIERARCHY
topics.plain: Noam Chomsky organized all computational languages into four nested tiers, each defined by specific grammar rules and recognized by a corresponding computational machine.
topics.def: The Chomsky Hierarchy establishes: Type 3 (Regular) subsetneq Type 2 (Context-Free) subsetneq Type 1 (Context-Sensitive) subsetneq Type 0 (Unrestricted / Recursively Enumerable). (1) Type 3: Rules A -> aB or A -> a, recognized by Finite Automata; (2) Type 2: Rules A -> alpha (LHS is single variable), recognized by Pushdown Automata; (3) Type 1: Rules alpha -> beta with |alpha| <= |beta| (except S -> epsilon), recognized by Linear Bounded Automata; (4) Type 0: Rules alpha -> beta without length restriction, recognized by Turing Machines.
topics.exam: All inclusions in the Chomsky hierarchy are STRICT: Type 3 (a^n) < Type 2 (a^n b^n) < Type 1 (a^n b^n c^n) < Type 0 (HALT_TM). Type 1, 2, and 3 are all decidable; Type 0 includes undecidable languages.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Assuming Context-Sensitive grammars allow shrinking productions. Type 1 productions alpha -> beta require |alpha| <= |beta| (non-contracting), ensuring tape space never shrinks below string length.
topics.example: L1 = {a^n} is Type 3; L2 = {a^n b^n} is Type 2; L3 = {a^n b^n c^n} is Type 1; L4 = {<M, w> | M halts on w} is Type 0.
topics.q: What are the four tiers of the Chomsky Hierarchy, along with their corresponding abstract recognizing machines?
topics.a: Type 3: Regular (Finite Automata); Type 2: Context-Free (Pushdown Automata); Type 1: Context-Sensitive (Linear Bounded Automata); Type 0: Unrestricted/RE (Turing Machines).

topics.title: COMPLEXITY CLASSES: P VS NP
topics.sub: Deterministic Polynomial Time vs Non-Deterministic Verification
topics.plain: Class P contains problems that can be SOLVED quickly (polynomial time). Class NP contains problems whose proposed solutions can be VERIFIED quickly.
topics.def: Complexity definitions: (1) Class P = bigcup_{k>=1} DTIME(n^k) is the class of decision problems decidable by a Deterministic Turing Machine in polynomial time O(n^k); (2) Class NP = bigcup_{k>=1} NTIME(n^k) is the class of decision problems decidable by a Non-Deterministic TM in polynomial time, or equivalently, problems for which a 'yes' certificate can be verified by a deterministic TM in polynomial time; (3) P subseteq NP is known; whether P = NP remains the foremost open problem in computer science.
topics.exam: Verification definition: Language L in NP iff there exists a polynomial-time verifier V and polynomial p such that w in L <=> exists certificate c with |c| <= p(|w|) such that V(w, c) accepts in polynomial time.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Defining NP as 'Non-Polynomial time'. NP stands for 'Non-deterministic Polynomial time', NOT non-polynomial! Every problem in P is also in NP (P subseteq NP).
topics.example: Sorting an array is in P (O(n log n)). Determining if a graph has a Hamiltonian cycle is in NP (given a vertex path certificate, verifying it takes linear time O(V + E)).
topics.q: What is the formal dual definition of the complexity class NP?
topics.a: NP is the class of languages decidable in polynomial time by a Non-Deterministic TM, or equivalently, verifiable in polynomial time by a Deterministic TM given a certificate.

topics.title: NP-COMPLETENESS & THE COOK-LEVIN THEOREM
topics.sub: Polynomial Reductions & SAT as the Hardest Problem in NP
topics.plain: NP-Complete problems are the hardest problems in NP. If ANY single NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time, then EVERY problem in NP can be solved in polynomial time (P = NP)!
topics.def: A language B is NP-Complete if: (1) B in NP; and (2) B is NP-Hard (for every language A in NP, A <=_p B via polynomial-time reduction). Cook-Levin Theorem (1971): The Boolean Satisfiability problem (SAT) is NP-Complete. By reducing SAT to 3-SAT, and 3-SAT to other problems (Clique, Vertex Cover, Hamiltonian Path, Subset Sum), Richard Karp established the core web of NP-complete problems.
topics.exam: To prove a new problem X is NP-Complete: (1) Prove X in NP (show a poly-time verifier exists); (2) Pick a known NP-Complete problem Y (e.g. 3-SAT); (3) Construct a polynomial-time reduction Y <=_p X; (4) Prove the reduction is correct in both directions.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Proving X <=_p Y when attempting to show X is NP-complete. To prove X is NP-complete, you must reduce FROM known problem Y TO new problem X (Y <=_p X)!
topics.example: 3-SAT reduces to Vertex Cover: each clause becomes a triangle of 3 vertices, and edges ensure satisfying assignments correspond to minimal vertex covers.
topics.q: What two conditions must a computational problem B satisfy to be classified as NP-Complete?
topics.a: 1. B must be in NP; and 2. B must be NP-Hard (every problem A in NP must be polynomial-time reducible to B: A <=_p B).

topics.title: APPLICATIONS OF AUTOMATA THEORY
topics.sub: Lexers, Parsers, Regular Expressions & Model Checking
topics.plain: Automata theory is not merely theoretical math; it is the practical engineering bedrock of software engineering, compiler construction, text search engines, and hardware verification.
topics.def: Primary real-world engineering applications of automata theory: (1) Compiler Frontends: Finite Automata drive lexical analyzers (Lex/Flex), Context-Free Grammars drive syntax parsers (Yacc/Bison, ANTLR, LR/LL parsers); (2) Pattern Matching: Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) string matching builds a DFA; Regular Expression engines in grep, sed, Python, JavaScript; (3) Hardware Design: Sequential logic circuits and Moore/Mealy state machines in FPGA/ASIC micro-architectures; (4) Formal Verification & Model Checking: Verifying concurrent protocols using Büchi automata over infinite words.
topics.exam: Compiler architecture mapping: Lexical Analysis = Regular Languages (Finite Automata); Syntax Analysis = Context-Free Languages (Pushdown Automata / CFG); Semantic Analysis & Code Generation = Turing Machine capability.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Believing syntax parsing in compilers uses finite automata. Parsing requires CFGs and pushdown automata because nested programming language structures (if/else, blocks, loops) exceed finite memory.
topics.example: The Unix command 'grep' uses a converted DFA (Thompson's construction + subset construction) to search multi-gigabyte text logs in linear time.
topics.q: How do the phases of a compiler map directly to the classes of the Chomsky Hierarchy?
topics.a: Lexical Analysis maps to Type 3 (Regular / Finite Automata); Syntax Analysis maps to Type 2 (Context-Free / Pushdown Automata); Semantic Analysis & Code Generation map to Type 0 (Turing Machines).

quiz.q: Alan Turing's proof of the undecidability of the Halting Problem demonstrates that:
opts: No general algorithm can exist that decides whether an arbitrary program halts on a given input
Turing machines cannot halt on inputs of length greater than their state count
Any program with a while loop is guaranteed to loop forever
Non-deterministic Turing machines can solve the Halting Problem in exponential time
quiz.correctFb: Turing proved by contradiction (diagonalization) that it is mathematically impossible to construct an algorithm that decides whether an arbitrary Turing machine halts on an arbitrary input.
distractors: Turing machines routinely halt on inputs of any finite length; the state count does not limit input size.
While loops can easily terminate when conditions are satisfied; termination is undecidable only in general.
Non-deterministic Turing machines have the same computational power as deterministic TMs and cannot solve the Halting Problem.

quiz.q: According to Rice's Theorem, which of the following properties of a Turing Machine M is algorithmically DECIDABLE?
opts: Testing whether M has more than 10 states in its state set Q
Testing whether the language L(M) is empty (L(M) = phi)
Testing whether the language L(M) is a regular language
Testing whether the string '101' is accepted by M
quiz.correctFb: Rice's Theorem applies strictly to semantic properties of the language L(M). Testing whether M has > 10 states is a syntactic property of the machine's encoding, which is decidable by simply inspecting its state table.
distractors: Testing emptiness L(M) = phi is a non-trivial semantic property of L(M), hence undecidable by Rice's Theorem.
Testing if L(M) is regular is a non-trivial semantic property, hence undecidable by Rice's Theorem.
Testing if string '101' in L(M) is equivalent to the Acceptance problem A_TM, which is undecidable.

quiz.q: Under what condition is the Post Correspondence Problem (PCP) known to be DECIDABLE?
opts: When the alphabet Sigma contains exactly one symbol (|Sigma| = 1)
When the alphabet Sigma contains two binary symbols ({0, 1})
When the number of domino pairs k is greater than 10
When all string lengths are even
quiz.correctFb: When |Sigma| = 1 (unary alphabet), the problem reduces to matching string lengths, which can be expressed as a linear Diophantine equation that is decidable via basic integer arithmetic.
distractors: For binary alphabets |Sigma| = 2, PCP is provably undecidable.
Increasing the number of domino pairs preserves or increases undecidability.
Even string lengths do not restrict the computational undecidability of PCP.

quiz.q: Which of the following decision problems concerning Context-Free Grammars is UNDECIDABLE?
opts: Determining whether an arbitrary Context-Free Grammar G is ambiguous
Determining whether a given string w belongs to L(G) (membership)
Determining whether the language L(G) is empty (L(G) = phi)
Determining whether the language L(G) is finite
quiz.correctFb: Testing ambiguity in an arbitrary CFG is provably undecidable (via reduction from the Post Correspondence Problem). Membership, emptiness, and finiteness are all decidable for CFGs.
distractors: Membership (w in L(G)) is decidable in O(n^3) time using the CYK algorithm.
Emptiness (L(G) = phi) is decidable by checking if the start symbol S derives any terminal string.
Finiteness is decidable by detecting cycles in the variable dependency graph of a simplified grammar.

quiz.q: What is the correct hierarchical order of language classes in the Chomsky Hierarchy from smallest (most restricted) to largest?
opts: Regular subsetneq Context-Free subsetneq Context-Sensitive subsetneq Recursively Enumerable
Context-Free subsetneq Regular subsetneq Context-Sensitive subsetneq Unrestricted
Regular subsetneq Context-Sensitive subsetneq Context-Free subsetneq Recursively Enumerable
Recursively Enumerable subsetneq Context-Sensitive subsetneq Context-Free subsetneq Regular
quiz.correctFb: The Chomsky Hierarchy defines Type 3 (Regular) subsetneq Type 2 (Context-Free) subsetneq Type 1 (Context-Sensitive) subsetneq Type 0 (Recursively Enumerable), with every containment being strict.
distractors: Context-Free languages strictly contain all Regular languages, not vice versa.

The inverted ordering places the most expressive unrestricted languages as the smallest.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a decision problem to belong to the complexity class NP?
opts: Any proposed solution ('yes' certificate) can be verified in polynomial time by a Deterministic Turing Machine
The problem cannot be solved in polynomial time by any computer
The problem requires exponential time on a Non-Deterministic Turing Machine
The problem is provably undecidable
quiz.correctFb: By definition, NP is the class of decision problems for which a candidate solution ('certificate') can be verified in deterministic polynomial time (or solved in polynomial time by an NTM).
distractors: NP stands for Non-deterministic Polynomial time, not non-polynomial; problems in P are also in NP.
Problems in NP are solved in POLYNOMIAL time by an NTM, not exponential time.
All problems in NP are fully decidable (in fact, decidable in exponential time O(2^(n^k))). Undecidable problems are not in NP.

quiz.q: The Cook-Levin Theorem is a foundational landmark in theoretical computer science because it proved that:
opts: The Boolean Satisfiability problem (SAT) is NP-Complete
P is strictly equal to NP
The Halting Problem is in NP
All Context-Free Grammars can be parsed in linear time
quiz.correctFb: The Cook-Levin Theorem (1971) proved that SAT is NP-Complete by demonstrating that any non-deterministic polynomial-time TM computation can be encoded as a polynomial-sized Boolean formula.
distractors: Cook-Levin did not prove P = NP; the P vs NP question remains an open Millennium Prize Problem.
The Halting Problem is undecidable and therefore not in NP.
Parsing general CFGs takes O(n^3) time via CYK, not linear time.

quiz.q: To prove that a new computational problem X is NP-Complete, which of the following reduction steps is REQUIRED?
opts: Reduce a known NP-Complete problem Y to X in polynomial time (Y <=_p X) and show X is in NP
Reduce X to a known NP-Complete problem Y in polynomial time (X <=_p Y)
Show that X cannot be verified in polynomial time
Prove that X is undecidable using Turing reductions
quiz.correctFb: To prove X is NP-complete, you must show: (1) X in NP; and (2) X is NP-hard by establishing a polynomial-time reduction from a known NP-complete problem Y to X (Y <=_p X).
distractors: Reducing X to Y (X <=_p Y) only shows X is in NP; it does not prove X is NP-hard.
If X cannot be verified in polynomial time, X is not even in NP, contradicting NP-completeness.
NP-complete problems are decidable; proving X undecidable places it far outside NP.

quiz.q: If a problem A is reducible to problem B in polynomial time (A <=_p B), and problem B is known to be in class P, what conclusion can be drawn about problem A?
opts: Problem A is also in class P
Problem A is NP-Complete
Problem A is undecidable
No conclusion can be drawn about problem A
quiz.correctFb: A polynomial-time reduction preserves polynomial solvability: if B can be solved in polynomial time and A reduces to B in polynomial time, then A can be solved in polynomial time (A in P).
distractors: Problem A is in P, which does not imply NP-completeness unless P = NP.
Since B is in P (decidable), A must also be decidable; it cannot be undecidable.
A definitive conclusion CAN be drawn: A is in P.

quiz.q: In a compiler pipeline, which phase is mathematically modeled by Pushdown Automata and Context-Free Grammars?
opts: Syntax Analysis (Parser)
Lexical Analysis (Scanner)
Code Optimization
Target Machine Code Generation
quiz.correctFb: Syntax Analysis (Parsing) checks whether code conforms to the nested grammar rules of the language, which requires a Context-Free Grammar and an underlying Pushdown Automaton.
distractors: Lexical Analysis is modeled by Finite Automata and Regular Expressions.
Code Optimization involves control flow graph algorithms and dataflow analysis.
Code Generation maps intermediate representations to assembly/machine code, requiring full Turing completeness.

bossChallenges.scenario: [10 MARKS] University Exam Question: State the Halting Problem for Turing Machines (HALT_TM). Provide the complete formal proof of its undecidability using Cantor's diagonalization method and proof by contradiction. Discuss why this theorem establishes an absolute theoretical upper bound on automated software verification.
rubric: Formal definition of the Halting problem decision language: HALT_TM = {<M, w> | M is a TM and M halts on input w}.
Hypothetical assumption of halting decider H(<M, w>) and construction of adversarial machine D(<M>) that runs H(<M, <M>>) and inverts the outcome (loops if H accepts, halts if H rejects).
Derivation of the self-referential paradox when D is supplied its own description: D(<D>) halts if and only if D(<D>) loops forever, establishing the contradiction.
Thorough discussion of the impossibility of building universal static bug detectors or automated software verification tools that guarantee halting on all program codes.

bossChallenges.scenario: [5 MARKS] Practical Problem-Solving Scenario: State Rice's Theorem. Clearly distinguish between a semantic property of a language and a syntactic property of a Turing machine. Provide two concrete examples of each, explaining which are decidable and which are undecidable.
rubric: Formal mathematical statement of Rice's Theorem: any non-trivial semantic property of the language recognized by a Turing machine is undecidable.
Clear distinction showing semantic properties pertain to the language L(M) recognized by the machine, while syntactic properties pertain to the machine's encoding/structure <M>.
Two concrete examples of undecidable semantic properties (e.g. testing if L(M) = phi, or testing if L(M) is regular) with brief justification under Rice's Theorem.
Two concrete examples of decidable syntactic properties (e.g. testing if M has fewer than 10 states, or testing if state q3 is reachable on transition 0) with justification.
